doc.title: Konitz Lee — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Playing two-horn with Kenny Wheeler
summary: They talk about two-horn groups, Kenny Wheeler's unpredictable improvising and writing, and Tristano's use of two-five-ones.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: He’s one of the relatively few trumpet players that you’ve played in a two-horn situation with. You’ve done Miles of course and Kenny Wheeler. A Swedish trumpet player named Yan Allen.
Yeah, right. He was a good trumpet player.
How do you feel about playing in that kind of setting? Is it something you enjoy?
I enjoyed playing with Kenny very much. We made another record [with] a few of our tunes and [some] standards. He was always kind of unpredictable in a nice way.

He liked to improvise. He made some un-trumpet like sounds sometimes. He was a great writer, Kenny. That was a great feature of his. I just heard the Cologne Radio Orchestra, which is a fine orchestra, do a program of his music and it was really some nice writing.
His writing is really unique, his harmonic concept in particular.
And looking at the chord symbols it seems like every chord is plus eleven, whatever it is.
There’s seldom a two-five-one. His harmonic concept is something totally other.
Yeah. He studied with Russo. I don’t know how much he had to do that. I don’t remember Tristano talking about two-five-ones that much either. It was usually five-one.

Kenny I think said something about how he never mastered “BeBop.” He talked about Bebop in the same way that you have, kind of facetiously. It was too hard, blah blah blah. Maybe his viewpoint is not dissimilar from yours.

I don’t think I ever heard him play really straight ahead like that. [It] always had a personal turn to it in some way. I think a lot of the “free” playing that he did had to do with the kind of freedom that he had in his harmonic playing.
